1554-adieu:
Balzac's short tale opens in an old monastery, where two French officers of the Napoleonic wars meet a madwoman who haunts the place. One of them, Philippe de Sucy, recognises in her Stephanie, the woman he loved during the terrible retreat from Russia, when a river crossing parted them forever.

The story moves between the present ruin and the frozen past, as Philippe tries to restore Stephanie's memory with a staged return to that fatal day. Its ending is haunting and restrained. Adieu is one of Balzac's most moving short works, a tale of war, love, and a mind broken by horror.
20521-the-new-york-times-current-history:
The New York Times Current History was a monthly magazine that printed the documents and speeches of the European war. Each issue gathered official statements from the fighting nations. Readers could follow the war in the words of its makers.

This portion gives the Ottoman side. It prints declarations by the Grand Vizier and other Turkish authorities. Their efforts and policy, the statements insist, are so explicit that no doubt remains about their meaning. Such volumes let American readers weigh each government's case during the First World War, long before the history books settled.
adieu:
Honoré de Balzac opens with hunters crossing a stubble field near the forest of L'Isle-Adam, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation. The party rests at an old monastery, where a strange, silent woman appears. One of the hunters knows her story, and it reaches back to Napoleon's retreat from Russia.

The middle chapter, The Passage of the Beresina, recalls the army's crossing of that freezing river and the horror that broke the woman's mind. The final chapter, The Cure, shows her old lover rebuild the scene of the crossing in hope of restoring her memory. The cure works for a moment, and the price is terrible.
britannica-1911-emeu:
Emeu, from the Portuguese Ema, is a name that was applied in turn to each of the earlier-known ratite birds, but has settled on the form that lives in Australia. Until the late 18th century most writers gave the name to the bird now called the cassowary. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the Emeu article within it. It treats the cassowaries and emeus side by side.

The two groups look much alike and form the order Megistanes, found only in the Australian Region. Each contour feather seems double, its aftershaft being as long as the main shaft. Plain marks divide the families, though. Grown cassowaries bear a horny helmet, a partly bare neck with wattles, and a long claw on the inner toe. Emeus have no helmet, a feathered head, no wattles, and a claw of no special kind.
britannica-1911-eu:
Eu is a town of north-western France in Seine-Inférieure, on the river Bresle north-east of Rouen. Its 1906 population was 4,865, and the forest of Eu spreads south-east of it. Three buildings stand out. The Gothic church of St Laurent, of the 12th and 13th centuries, shows tiered buttressing on its choir. The Jesuit college chapel, built about 1625, holds the tombs of Henry, third duke of Guise, and Katherine of Cleves.

Henry of Guise began the château in 1578 on a site Louis XI had burnt in 1475. Mademoiselle de Montpensier carried it on, and Louis Philippe restored it. He received Queen Victoria there in 1843 and 1845. Fire gutted most of it in 1902. The town makes earthenware, biscuits, furniture and glass, and trades in grain and timber. Charles of Eu was held prisoner in England for twenty-three years after Agincourt.
britannica-1911-la-chaise-dieu:
La Chaise-Dieu is a town of central France, in the department of Haute Loire, 29 miles N.N.W. of Le Puy by rail. In 1906 it held 1203 people. The town stands among fir and pine woods, 3500 feet above the sea. It keeps remains of its ramparts and houses of the 14th and 15th centuries. Its fame rests on its church, after the cathedral of Clermont-Ferrand the finest Gothic building in Auvergne.

Two massive towers flank the west front. Nave and aisles stand at one height, cut off from the choir by a stone rood screen. The choir holds the fine tomb and statue of Clement VI, carved stalls, and Flemish tapestries of the early 16th century. The church dates from the 14th century and was built at the cost of Pope Clement VI. It belonged to a strong Benedictine abbey founded in 1043.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anatole-leroy:
Born at Lisieux in 1842, Anatole Leroy-Beaulieu died in Paris on 15 June 1912, after a career as a French publicist. A historical romance about the Italian risorgimento opened his writing life in 1866, and political and historical study followed. Collected in 1879, his essays on Napoleon III, Victor Emmanuel, and Pius IX still matter for the history of the second French Empire.

His 1874 protest against rebuilding Gothic cathedrals to fit set systems urged honest repair instead, and it showed striking originality. Three volumes on the tsars' empire and the Russians, published from 1883 to 1887, survey Russian religion and sects across the Slavic empire. He also wrote about serf emancipation under Alexander II and about French Liberal Catholics. From 1906 he directed the Free School of Political Science, where he had taught for a long time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-de-mont:
Baron de Montesquieu was a French writer and publicist, born near Bordeaux in 1689, who died at Paris in 1755. His grandfather presided over Bordeaux's Parliament, his father served the royal bodyguard, and his mother died when he was eleven. At Juilly's Oratorian College from 1700 to 1711, he gained a literary and classical education with little religion. At twenty-five, called to the bar, he took his uncle's title and became a Bordeaux Parliament councillor.

He married the Protestant Jeanne Lartigue, and they had three children, but neither profession nor family claimed much of him. After nine years he sold his office and gave himself wholly to study, his life's one passion. Study, he wrote, was his sovereign remedy against life's worries, dispelling any care within an hour's reading. His earliest works went before Bordeaux's Academy, which he joined in 1716, on science, history, and politics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal-rich:
Cardinal Richelieu was a French statesman born in Paris in September 1585 who died there in December 1642. He first aimed at a military career, but took the Bishopric of Luçon in 1605 when his brother Alfred retired to the Grande Chartreuse. Consecrated bishop in April 1607 before he turned twenty-two, he threw himself into converting Protestants in his diocese through Oratorian and Capuchin missions.

His political career opened at the States General of 1614, where he spoke for the clergy of Poitou and demanded bishops in royal councils. He also sought an end to lay grants of benefices and freedom of the Church from taxation. Later sections follow his long ministry, his patronage of letters, and his tangles with Rome. He headed the Sorbonne as proviseur from 1622 and had it rebuilt. He rebuffed the nuncio in October 1639.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-de-jussieu:
A family entry introduces the de Jussieus, five French botanists across three generations. Antoine, born at Lyons in 1686 and dead at Paris in 1758, studied medicine at Montpellier and succeeded Tournefort at the Jardin du Roi in 1708. He explored the flora of France and the Pyrenean peninsula, practised medicine among the poor, and introduced quassia bark, first sent from Cayenne in 1713.

His papers covered anatomy, zoology, palaeontology, and mineralogy, and his 1713 description of coffee holds historical value. Later de Jussieus carried the family science further: Bernard, Joseph, and Adrien, whose natural system of plant classification, Genera Plantarum of 1789, and botanical geography shaped modern botany. The entry follows each career with its publications and honours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-nepve:
Francis Nepveu, born at St. Malo on 29 April 1639 and dead at Rennes on 17 February 1708. He was a French Jesuit writer on the ascetical life, the practice of prayer and holiness. He entered the Jesuit novitiate on 12 October 1654, aged only fifteen, and taught grammar, humanities, and rhetoric for six years and philosophy for eight. He then worked in the government of his order, serving as superior at Nantes, rector at Vannes, Orleans, and Rouen, and at Rennes as director of retreats until his death.

 His work on the love of Jesus Christ and the means of acquiring it, published at Nantes in 1684, ran to fourteen French editions. It was translated into German, Italian, Spanish, Flemish, Polish, and English. His retreat after the spirit and method of St. Ignatius, published in 1677, also reached fourteen editions, with versions in five languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-desi:
Francois-Desire Mathieu, born on 27 May 1839 at Einville in Meurthe-et-Moselle and dead on 26 October 1908, was a French bishop and cardinal of humble birth. He studied at the diocesan school and Nancy seminary and was ordained in 1863. He taught at the minor seminary of Pont-a-Mousson, served as chaplain to the Dominican sisters at Nancy, and became parish priest of St. Martin at Pont-a-Mousson in 1890.

Nominated Bishop of Angers on 3 January 1893 and consecrated on 20 March, he succeeded the remarkable Freppel and kept all his predecessor's good works. He added help for poor boys destined for the priesthood. Transferred to Toulouse in 1896 by Leo XIII, he laboured to rally Catholics to the French government, writing Devoir des catholiques, an episcopal charge that drew wide attention and the pope's congratulations. He was later summoned to Rome as a cardinal of the Curia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-de-gon:
Jérôme de Gonnelieu, a French Jesuit theologian, spiritual writer, and preacher born at Soissons in 1640 and dead in Paris in 1715. He entered the Society at seventeen and taught with marked skill until his final vows in 1674. From then on the pulpit claimed him.

Gonnelieu won repute as a sacred orator with a rare gift: putting the loftiest spiritual thoughts into words ordinary people could grasp. Many sought him as counsellor and guide, and his duties were done with thorough self-sacrifice. Late in life he turned to books, above all an Exercise of the Spiritual Life in 1701 and a work on God's presence as the heart of inner life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vizeu:
Viseu is a diocese in north-central Portugal whose bishopric dates from the sixth century and has counted eighty-three bishops, including doubtful prelates and those elected but unconfirmed. Its list begins with Remissol, 572 to 585, who attended Braga's second council but was exiled by the Arian king Leovigild, followed by Tunila.

Abjured Arianism at Toledo's third council, with Viseu bishops present at Toledo's fourth, sixth, eighth, twelfth, and thirteenth councils. After a fifteen-year vacancy from 665 to 680 and Theofredo in 693, Saracen invasion left Viseu without a bishop for nearly two centuries. Theodomiro attended Santiago de Compostela's consecration in 876 and Oviedo's council in 877, and after seventy-six years of Moorish occupation its prelates Gomes and Sisnando resided at Oviedo. From 1110 to 1144 priors appointed by Coimbra's bishops governed it, among them St Theotonio, later the city's patron, before the episcopal line resumed with Odorio.
doe-osti-3003153-symmetry-determining-eq:
Patrick Francis O'Rourke of Los Alamos derives equations in report LA-UR-25-31247, issued November 14, 2025. The subject is symmetry analysis of the Euler equations, the core equations of fluid flow. Symmetries let analysts shrink a hard problem to a simpler one, or solve it outright. The document supplements his earlier lecture volume on solving differential equations with Lie group theory.

O'Rourke works through the derivation of the symmetry determining equations step by step. He then presents the full Lie algebra for the Euler system. Worked examples show reductions of the equations and cases where closed-form solutions fall out. The intended readers are students and code physicists who use analytic solutions to check simulations. Clear derivations matter here because a single sign error quietly invalidates every solution built on top.
doe-osti-3019794-hpdf-data-catalog-and-l:
Hannah Cohoon and Drew Paine of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory evaluated a data platform's usability in LBNL-2001745, drafted December 2025 and revised February 2026. The HPDF project was demonstrating a data catalog and a lakehouse demo. The user experience team assessed both twice over: a heuristic evaluation by experts, and a roadshow collecting stakeholder feedback. Findings are concrete. In one example, a file named dfit-pump.csv sits beside a related iceberg table named dfit_pump_csv. Users had to search to discover that the two were related.

That friction is the report's theme: scientific data services fail at findability before they fail at storage. Each finding pairs the problem with screenshots in an appendix. For the HPDF team, the reports convert frustration into a fix list while the platform is new. The document is peer reviewed and posted through UC Berkeley's eScholarship. Other data projects can borrow its evaluation format.
podcast-dannyjones-W8VsdzG1KeU:
Tony Lyons joins Danny Jones to argue that Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is exposing a hidden CIA tool for shaping minds. The episode title calls that tool a psychological weapon. Lyons speaks as the guest, and Jones hosts the talk.

The guest lays out claims about how the agency has used media and culture to steer public thought. He links those claims to Kennedy's public fight with the agency and its allies. The episode keeps the tone of a warning from an insider's ally. The library holds it as an archive record, and listeners can weigh the claims on their own terms.
podcast-dannyjones-k2UCiBNwteU:
Climate scholar Henrik Svensmark joins Danny Jones to claim he was banned after he found the truth about clouds. Svensmark worked at CERN-linked labs on how the sun and space rays shape clouds. His claim is that the field shut him out.

Svensmark explains his tests and how clouds may drive more of the climate than most models grant. He tells how doors closed on his work once it cut against the main view. Jones asks what fair tests would look like. Listeners get the case of a man the field pushed aside. The library files the talk as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-FApCVOXoweU:
Dr. Rhonda Patrick returns for episode 672 of the Joe Rogan Experience, a mid-run entry in her years as the show's health-science regular. Patrick researches how food, heat, and exercise change the body at the level of cells and genes. Her talks are dense, and listeners come ready to take notes.

She updates Rogan on the findings she finds strongest, from supplements under study to the effects of sauna and fasting. Rogan presses her on what a normal person should actually do Monday morning. The episode shows the pair's routine at its best: hard science, translated live, with the caveats left in.
podcast-joerogan-JOi2Pl-lBeU:
Director Stanley Kubrick and the claim that he helped fake the moon landing fill a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. The theory holds that NASA hired the master filmmaker to stage the Apollo footage. Rogan treats the idea as an archive claim to examine, not a fact to endorse.

The talk reviews the usual evidence offered, from shadows in photos to Kubrick's own films, and the replies skeptics give. Rogan asks why the story grips people who trust nothing else they are told. The segment preserves a famous piece of moon-landing lore, with its best arguments laid out for listeners to weigh.
